entities.name: Aaronic Priesthood
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Aaronic Priesthood (also called the Levitical Priesthood) was the hereditary priestly order established by God through Moses, with Aaron — Moses' elder brother — as its first High Priest. Instituted at Mount Sinai (c. 1446 BCE), the priesthood was confined exclusively to Aaron's male descendants from the tribe of Levi. Aaron and his sons were consecrated in a seven-day ordination ceremony involving anointing oil, sacrificial blood, and sacred vestments (Exodus 29).

The High Priest alone entered the Holy of Holies once per year on Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) to sprinkle blood on the mercy seat of the Ark of the Covenant. The priesthood maintained the daily tamid offering, the incense altar, the showbread, and the menorah in the Tabernacle and later in Solomon's Temple. The Aaronic line produced notable figures including Eleazar, Phinehas, Eli, Zadok (whose descendants served in the First and Second Temples), and Ezra the Scribe.

The institution shaped Israelite worship for over a millennium until the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, after which rabbinic Judaism replaced priestly sacrifice with prayer and Torah study. The Epistle to the Hebrews presents Jesus Christ as a superior High Priest after the order of Melchizedek, superseding the Aaronic order.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Aaronic Priesthood played a crucial role in the development of Judaism and early Christianity, with its rituals and practices influencing the formation of Western religious traditions. The priesthood's daily offerings and sacred ceremonies helped establish a sense of community and ritual practice among ancient Israelites.
